# Shorthand (stenography) (`shorthand`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/communication.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Communication & information (`communication`)
- Deps: helped by alphabet_writing
- Core idea: A script of very simple strokes, one per sound, with vowels left out or shown by position and fixed signs for the commonest words, so a trained writer keeps up with speech (over 100 words a minute). With it, debates, trials, sermons and lectures can be recorded word for word and checked later. It must be a fixed published system that others can read, and transcribed into ordinary writing soon after.
- Pitfalls:
  - Inventing personal abbreviations: nobody else, and soon not even the writer, can read them
  - Basing it on spelling rather than sound: English spelling makes that slow
  - Expecting quick results: it takes months of daily practice
- History: greece: 4th c. BC – an inscription from the Athenian Acropolis describes a shorthand system; rome: 63 BC – Plutarch says that Cicero stationed trained shorthand writers to record Cato’s Senate speech; the later shorthand tradition names Cicero’s freedman Tiro; europe: 1588 – Timothy Bright's Characterie; 1660s Pepys keeps his diary in Shelton's shorthand; 1834 Gabelsberger (German); 1837 Isaac Pitman's phonetic system; 1888 Gregg publishes Light-Line Phonography in Liverpool; americas: 1890s – Gregg promotes his shorthand in the United States
- Read:
  - Plutarch, Cato the Younger 23 (c. AD 100)
  - Isaac Pitman, Stenographic Sound-Hand (1837)
